title: Lp(a) Testing and Risk Assessment
answer: Because Lp(a) is mostly inherited and fairly stable, guidelines now recommend measuring it at least once in adulthood, ideally reported in nmol/L. One test usually suffices; a high result should prompt more intensive control of other risk factors and testing of close relatives.

sections.body: Ask for the test, ask which unit the lab used, and if your level is high, tell your parents, siblings and children.
sections.heading: What it means for patients

explainer:
Laboratories report Lp(a) either as mass, in mg/dL, or as particle number, in nmol/L. Because apolipoprotein(a) comes in many sizes, the mass of a particle varies between people, so there is no single exact conversion between the two units. Rough conversions are useful for orientation, but a result should be interpreted in the unit it was measured in, and nmol/L assays are preferred.

Risk rises steadily with level rather than switching on at a threshold, so cutoffs are guides. Very high levels carry risk comparable to familial hypercholesterolaemia. Testing is especially useful for people with premature heart disease, a family history of early heart attack or stroke, familial hypercholesterolaemia, aortic stenosis, or heart disease despite controlled LDL.

developments.text: A 2026 review notes major societies recommend every adult have Lp(a) measured at least once, echoed by 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidaemia guidance, with standardised reporting in nmol/L where available.

The European Atherosclerosis Society consensus set practical cutoffs: below 30 mg/dL (about 75 nmol/L) to rule out and above 50 mg/dL (about 125 nmol/L) to rule in Lp(a) related risk, with a grey zone between.
